objectives: Organize white-noise stimuli, spike trains, and the spike-triggered ensemble into a system-identification workflow, distinguishing a descriptive STA, a filter estimator, and a complete LNP component.
Move among continuous convolution, pixel-index summation, and matrix notation while tracking the shapes of S, K, L, and the count vector and the orientation of the time-lag axis.
Derive the normal equation and Hessian from mean-squared loss for a linear neuron, and explain circular versus elongated loss contours through stimulus covariance.
Starting from SS^T≈Tσ_s^2I, derive the proportionality between K̂ and the STA while retaining the scaling by spike count, bin width, and stimulus variance.

prerequisiteBridge: An LNP model first takes the inner product between stimulus-history vector s_t∈R^{P×1} and filter K∈R^{P×1}, giving L_t=K^Ts_t, and then maps L_t through nonlinearity F to a rate. P may flatten pixels together with x, y, and several past time lags into one index. Every experimental time bin supplies one column s_t, so the design matrix is S∈R^{P×T}.

Least squares chooses K so that S^TK approximates measured response h. Its gradient is -S(h-S^TK)/T; setting it to zero gives SS^TK=Sh. The Hessian SS^T/T describes loss curvature along filter directions. If one stimulus direction is scarcely sampled, its curvature is small and the filter estimate becomes highly noise-sensitive.

Here white noise means that distinct pixel/time dimensions are approximately zero-mean, uncorrelated, and equal-variance, so the large-sample covariance approaches σ_s^2I. With sufficiently small bins, spike count k_t is usually 0 or 1 and P(k_t=1|L_t)≈ΔtF(L_t). The STA averages stimulus vectors preceding spike bins, all aligned to the same lags.

diagnostic.prompt: What does column t of S∈R^{P×T} represent, and why is K^TS_{:t} a scalar?
diagnostic.answer: It is the stimulus history preceding time t, flattened in a fixed lag order. K and that column are both P-dimensional, so their inner product is one linear drive.
diagnostic.explanation: Each time bin is one high-dimensional regression example. Placing time in rows while retaining the original formulas misaligns the orientations of K, S, and the response.

diagnostic.prompt: What experimental problem is indicated by a small eigenvalue of the least-squares Hessian H=SS^T/T?
diagnostic.answer: The stimulus varies little along that eigenvector direction, so loss curvature is weak and the data constrain that filter component poorly.
diagnostic.explanation: Many K values displaced along that direction give almost identical predictions, leaving the estimate dominated by measurement noise or regularization. Identifiability improves only by adding stimulus variation in that direction.

diagnostic.prompt: Why are loss contours nearly circular, rather than tilted ellipses, for large-sample equal-variance white noise?
diagnostic.answer: Because H≈σ_s^2I, all orthogonal filter directions have equal curvature and cross-terms are nearly zero.
diagnostic.explanation: The identity matrix favors no coordinate direction. Finite samples still create off-diagonal fluctuations, so circularity is an approximation rather than exact geometry in every experiment.

diagnostic.prompt: A neuron fires strongly when |K^Ts| is large and responds identically to positive and negative projections. Why can its linear STA be nearly zero?
diagnostic.answer: Stimuli resembling +K and -K both precede spikes, and the two groups cancel in their vector average.
diagnostic.explanation: A zero first moment does not imply an absence of stimulus dependence. Spike-triggered covariance can reveal increased variance along K, and an energy model can represent this even response.

modules.title: White-Noise System Identification in Three Notations
modules.guidingQuestion: Given a complete stimulus movie and spike times, how can the stimulus history before each spike be converted into a dataset for estimating a filter?
paragraphs: System identification reverses forward prediction. A forward LNP model predicts spikes from known K and F; the experiment supplies stimulus s and spikes k and seeks K and F. The standard protocol in the source notes presents random checkerboard white noise, records neural spikes, looks backward from every spike over the same time lags, and averages those stimulus histories. Stimulus coordinates, frame duration, and neural latency must be defined first.

The spike-triggered ensemble contains every stimulus vector that preceded a spike, and its mean is the STA. For an ON-center RGC, the most recent lag may show a bright center and dark surround, while an earlier lag may differ in sign or shape, producing a biphasic temporal kernel. Every history must be aligned to its spike; otherwise alignment error artificially smears the filter in addition to true latency variation.

Continuous notation writes L(t)=∫dx' dy' dt' K(x',y',t')s(x',y',t-t'). After discretization, combine (x,y,t') into index p to obtain L_t=Σ_pK_pS_{pt}. Matrix notation is L=S^TK. All three forms express the same inner product. Matrix form is convenient for least squares, whereas continuous form shows spatial location and causal lag directly.

Each column of S is an entire stimulus history, not just the current frame; the p entries of K follow the same flattening order. Reversing the lag index flips the estimated kernel in time. A white-noise protocol matters not because the pattern merely looks random, but because different dimensions have nearly diagonal sample covariance on a common scale, reducing estimator bias and uneven uncertainty.
keyPoints: An STA requires identical stimulus-history alignment at every spike; averaging only the spike frame is insufficient.
Continuous convolution, a pixel sum, and S^TK are alternative representations of the same calculation.
The defining benefit of white noise is covariance isotropy, not an arbitrarily generated noisy picture.

derivation.title: Discretizing Spatiotemporal Convolution as S^TK
derivation.setup: Use N_x×N_y pixels and N_τ causal lags, for total dimension P=N_xN_yN_τ; the experiment contains T usable time bins.

steps.title: Define a Compound Index
steps.explanation: Assign a unique p to every (x_i,y_j,τ_q), write K(x_i,y_j,τ_q) as K_p, and write the past stimulus s(x_i,y_j,t-τ_q) corresponding to time t as S_{pt}.

steps.title: Replace the Integral with a Grid-Volume-Weighted Sum
steps.explanation: Spatial and temporal discretization introduces the factor ΔxΔyΔτ. Absorbing it into K_p leaves an ordinary dot product.

steps.title: Stack All Time Bins into a Vector
steps.explanation: S^T is T×P; multiplying it by P×1 vector K produces T×1 vector L, with each row reproducing one time-bin inner product.

symbolNotes: In this lecture T denotes sample count but is also commonly used for physical time. Within matrix shapes it means the number of bins, and explanations should keep the meanings distinct.
The time coordinate of K is look-back lag: τ=0 is the current or most recent bin, and positive τ refers to earlier stimuli.
derivation.unitsCheck: If continuous K has units drive/(contrast·area·time), multiplying by contrast and dx dy dτ gives drive. If discrete K absorbs grid volume, its numerical units depend on binning.
derivation.limitCheck: A frame rate that is too low aliases fast temporal structure. A history window that is too short truncates the kernel; one that is too long increases P and reduces statistical power per dimension.

workedExample.title: Matrix Prediction with Two Pixels and Four Time Bins
workedExample.problem: Let S=[[1,-1,1,-1],[1,1,-1,-1]] and K=(2,1)^T. Compute L=S^TK and interpret each entry.
steps: At t1 the stimulus is (1,1), so L1=2×1+1×1=3; at t2 it is (-1,1), so L2=-2+1=-1.
At t3 the stimulus is (1,-1), so L3=2-1=1; at t4 it is (-1,-1), so L4=-2-1=-3.
Therefore L=(3,-1,1,-3)^T. The first pixel has the larger weight, so changing its coordinate affects the drive more strongly.
workedExample.result: One matrix multiplication computes the filter projections for all four time bins while preserving the pairing with each stimulus column.
workedExample.sanityCheck: S is 2×4 and S^T is 4×2; multiplication by 2×1 K must yield 4×1. A 2-dimensional result signals that the orientation has been reversed.

selfCheck.prompt: Why must each member of the spike-triggered ensemble contain a stimulus history rather than only the frame in which the spike occurs?
selfCheck.answer: Neural responses have latency and may depend on multiple past lags. Using only the current frame discards temporal filtering and attaches the causal feature to the wrong spike time. A history vector permits simultaneous estimation of spatial and temporal receptive-field structure.

pitfalls: Flattening the stimulus without recording pixel and lag order, so the resulting vector cannot be reshaped correctly into a receptive field.
Calling a stimulus white merely because it looks random, without checking its mean, variance, cross-correlations, and finite-sample covariance.

modules.title: Least Squares, the Hessian, and White-Noise Isotropy
modules.guidingQuestion: Why does stimulus covariance control uncertainty in a filter estimate, and how does white noise place different feature directions on a common scale?
paragraphs: First consider a linear neuron h_t≈K^Ts_t, where h may be a measured firing-rate estimate. Mean-squared loss averages prediction error over T bins. Setting gradient=0 gives the normal equation SS^TK=Sh: stimulus covariance scale times the filter equals stimulus-response cross-correlation. Identifiability depends on whether S spans the relevant directions.

For a linear model with quadratic loss, the Hessian H=SS^T/T is independent of K. Its eigenvectors are the principal axes of the loss ellipse and its eigenvalues are curvatures. Along a large-eigenvalue direction, a small change in K noticeably changes predictions and the data tightly constrain the minimum. Along a small-eigenvalue direction, the loss is flat and recording noise, finite samples, or regularization can move the estimate substantially.

In ideal Gaussian white stimulation, every S_{pt} has zero mean and variance σ_s^2, and different p dimensions are uncorrelated. At large T, (SS^T)_{pq}=Σ_tS_{pt}S_{qt}≈Tσ_s^2δ_{pq}. Consequently H≈σ_s^2I, the loss contours are nearly circular, and every filter dimension has equal curvature.

A finite dataset never has covariance exactly equal to the identity: off-diagonal sample covariances fluctuate around zero. Unequal pixel variances produce a diagonal but anisotropic H. With colored stimuli, correlations in H cause raw cross-correlation to mix the true filter with the stimulus spectrum. One must then apply the covariance inverse explicitly, whiten the stimulus, or fit a regularized likelihood model.
keyPoints: The normal equation expresses filter estimation as inverse covariance applied to stimulus-response correlation.
A Hessian eigenvalue measures both loss curvature and identifiability along its filter direction.
White-noise isotropy is a large-sample approximation; colored stimuli require covariance correction.

derivation.title: The Normal Equation and an Isotropic Hessian
derivation.setup: Define L(K)=(1/2T)||h-S^TK||^2, with S∈R^{P×T} and h∈R^{T×1}.

steps.title: Compute the Gradient
steps.explanation: For residual r=h-S^TK, derivatives of prediction along the filter coordinates are supplied by S, so the gradient is -S times the residual.

steps.title: Compute the Estimate and Hessian
steps.explanation: Setting gradient=0 yields SS^TK=Sh. Differentiating the gradient once more gives H=SS^T/T.

steps.title: Insert the White Covariance
steps.explanation: For independent, equal-variance dimensions, off-diagonal sample sums approach zero and diagonal sums approach Tσ_s^2, so the inverse is approximately (Tσ_s^2)^{-1}I.

symbolNotes: H is a P×P curvature matrix; it is neither neural-response covariance nor spike-triggered covariance.
δ_{pq} is the Kronecker delta: it equals 1 for p=q and 0 otherwise, encoding ideal white covariance.
derivation.unitsCheck: SS^T has units stimulus^2 and Sh has units stimulus×response. The resulting estimate therefore has units response/stimulus, as required for linear-filter gain.
derivation.limitCheck: If T≤P or stimulus dimensions are linearly dependent, SS^T may be singular and the inverse expression cannot be used directly.

workedExample.title: Recovering a Known Filter from a White Design
workedExample.problem: Continue with S=[[1,-1,1,-1],[1,1,-1,-1]], true K=(2,1)^T, and h=S^TK=(3,-1,1,-3)^T. Recover K by least squares.
steps: SS^T=[[4,0],[0,4]]=4I, showing that the two stimulus dimensions have isotropic sample covariance.
Sh=(8,4)^T; for example, its first entry is 1×3+(-1)×(-1)+1×1+(-1)×(-3)=8.
K̂=(4I)^{-1}(8,4)^T=(2,1)^T, exactly recovering the true filter.
workedExample.result: For orthogonal equal-variance stimuli, the covariance inverse supplies only a common rescaling, so the direction of the cross-correlation is the filter direction.
workedExample.sanityCheck: If the second stimulus row is replaced by a copy of the first, SS^T has rank 1. Only the sum of the two filter weights affects prediction, so the weights cannot be identified separately.

selfCheck.prompt: Why does an elongated loss contour indicate that some filter combinations are estimated unreliably?
selfCheck.answer: Moving along the ellipse's long axis raises loss only slightly. This is a small-eigenvalue direction of the Hessian, where many different K values make similar predictions on the sampled stimuli, allowing finite noise to shift the minimum substantially.

pitfalls: Interpreting a circular loss contour as a circular receptive field; the contour describes curvature in parameter space, not spatial shape.
Using the white-noise approximation without the large-T, equal-variance, and independence assumptions.

modules.title: From the Kernel Estimate to the STA, Nonlinearity, and Failure Diagnostics
modules.guidingQuestion: Under which scaling and probabilistic assumptions does the stimulus average before spikes point along a linear filter, and what kinds of selectivity can this average cancel completely?
paragraphs: The data contain spike counts k_t rather than a continuous rate h_t. Choose bin width Δt small enough that k_t∈{0,1} usually holds and define rate estimate h_t=k_t/Δt. Then Sh=(1/Δt)Σ_{t:k_t=1}s_t, the sum of spike-triggered stimulus vectors scaled by bin width.

Because STA=(1/n_sp)Σ_{spikes}s_t, a white design gives K̂≈[n_sp/(Tσ_s^2Δt)]STA. STA and K point in the same direction, but absolute amplitude depends on spike count, recording duration, stimulus variance, and bin width. Comparing raw STA amplitudes across cells or conditions can therefore mistake a firing-rate change for a filter-gain change.

After estimating K̂, compute L_t=K̂^Ts_t in every time bin, group values into bins of L, and estimate empirical P(spike|L). The small-bin Poisson approximation gives P(k=1|L)≈ΔtF(L), hence F̂(L)=P(spike|L)/Δt. Finally combine K̂, F̂, and the Poisson stage on held-out stimuli and compare predicted with observed spikes; a training STA alone is not a model test.

STA succeeds when one linear dimension dominates, the stimulus distribution is suitable, and spike count is adequate. Colored stimulation biases its direction; non-Gaussian input breaks the simple proportionality; multiple relevant dimensions collapse into one average; an even nonlinearity F(L)=F(-L) cancels +K and -K ensembles; and history dependence or adaptation contaminates the stimulus filter. Thus STA=0 is not evidence for “no receptive field.”
keyPoints: The proportionality between K̂ and STA contains n_sp, T, σ_s^2, and Δt; their directional relation is more robust than raw amplitude.
Estimate the nonlinearity by dividing projection-conditioned spike probability by bin width.
An even response, multiple relevant dimensions, and colored stimulation can bias an STA or make it zero.

derivation.title: STA Proportionality with All Scale Factors Retained
derivation.setup: Assume white stimulation SS^T≈Tσ_s^2I, bin counts k_t∈{0,1}, rate estimate h_t=k_t/Δt, and n_sp spike bins.

steps.title: Rewrite Response Cross-Correlation as a Spike Sum
steps.explanation: Bins with k_t=0 contribute nothing; bins with k_t=1 retain stimulus vector s_t and carry scale 1/Δt.

steps.title: Introduce the Definition of STA
steps.explanation: The spike sum equals spike count times the mean spike-triggered stimulus.

steps.title: Substitute the Least-Squares Estimate
steps.explanation: The covariance inverse contributes the common factor 1/(Tσ_s^2), yielding the proportionality between filter and STA.

symbolNotes: n_sp/TΔt is the mean firing rate, so the proportionality factor can also be written mean rate/σ_s^2.
STA entries have stimulus units. K̂ as a rate filter is additionally divided by stimulus variance, so their gain units differ.
derivation.unitsCheck: n_sp/(TΔt) has units 1/time; dividing by σ_s^2 and multiplying by stimulus gives rate/stimulus, as required for a linear rate filter.
derivation.limitCheck: If bins are too wide, k_t can exceed 1 and the Bernoulli simplification fails. With too few spikes, STA variance is large even when the expectation relation holds.

workedExample.title: How an Even Nonlinearity Makes the STA Vanish
workedExample.problem: A one-dimensional stimulus s takes -1, 0, or +1 with equal prior probability. The neuron spikes with probability 0.4 at s=±1 and 0.1 at s=0. Compute the spike-triggered mean and second moment and compare them with the original stimulus variance.
steps: The total spike probability is (0.4+0.1+0.4)/3=0.3. Bayes' rule gives P(s=-1|spike)=4/9, P(s=0|spike)=1/9, and P(s=+1|spike)=4/9.
The positive and negative endpoints have equal conditional weight, so STA=E[s|spike]=(-1)(4/9)+0+(+1)(4/9)=0.
The spike-triggered second moment is E[s^2|spike]=(4/9)+(4/9)=8/9. Because the conditional mean is zero, this is also the spike-triggered variance.
The original stimulus has zero mean and variance E[s^2]=2/3. Spike-triggered variance increases by 8/9-2/3=2/9, revealing a preference for large |s|.
workedExample.result: The STA is zero, yet spike-triggered variance rises from 2/3 to 8/9. STC or a quadratic model can detect the relevant direction hidden by symmetric averaging over signs.
workedExample.sanityCheck: The three conditional probabilities sum to 1. If the spike probabilities at ±1 are changed to equal that at s=0, the spike-triggered distribution returns to the prior and the variance difference becomes zero.

selfCheck.prompt: Why is a smooth increasing F̂(L) curve on the training data insufficient evidence that an LNP model predicts?
selfCheck.answer: Both K and F were estimated from the same data, and binning plus a flexible curve can absorb noise. Generalization must be tested by computing projections on held-out stimuli and predicting conditional rates or spikes there.

pitfalls: Comparing raw STA amplitudes across conditions without correcting for spike rate, stimulus variance, duration, and bin width.
Reading STA=0 as proof that a neuron is not stimulus-selective while ignoring even nonlinearities and multiple-feature coding.
